title: The first read — Image Wiki
text:
The first read
  What is left of a poster when you are far away and not paying attention — and the five or six tests that tell you whether that residue still carries the message.

  
    Termfirst read / legibility at distance
    Also calledthumbnail test, squint test, three-metre test, stopping power
    Not the same asvisual hierarchy, minimalism, font legibility
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        What actually limits youThe testsThe same test, other objectsWhat survives, roughly in orderCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Walk to the far side of the room from your screen and look back at the last poster or thumbnail you judged. Most of it is gone. A big shape, maybe a colour, maybe one word. That residue is the first read, and it is the only part of a poster a stranger is guaranteed to receive.
The first read is the testable half of poster design. Whether the joke lands or the photograph is beautiful is arguable; whether the title survives at 8% size in a phone grid is not — you look, and either it does or it does not.



Arthur Rothstein, See America — Welcome to Montana, United States Travel Bureau, made by the Works Progress Administration Federal Art Project, New York, between 1936 and 1938. Public domain (Library of Congress).
Squint at this, or scroll until it is thumbnail-sized, and count what is left: one big rust-brown mountain silhouette, a pale sky, a blue band of water, a pale teepee and a dark one at the bottom left, and two lines of type. Almost nothing in the picture is drawn — it is built from flat areas of six colours, and every boundary between two areas is also a value step, light against dark, so the shapes hold when the colour is stripped out. The only drawn marks in the whole sheet are the thin petroglyph figures on the pale teepee, and they are second-read material.
Then look at what the poster gave up to get that. There is no texture, no modelling, no detail small enough to reward standing close. The second read here is thin on purpose: this sheet was made to work on a wall you walk past.


What actually limits you
Two separate ceilings, and people confuse them constantly.
Resolution. Normal vision resolves detail about one arcminute wide. At three metres that is 0.9 mm; at one metre, 0.3 mm. To identify a letter you need it to subtend roughly five arcminutes — about 4 mm of cap height at three metres — and to read a line of unfamiliar text comfortably you want several times that. So 10 pt caption type, whose capitals are about 2.5 mm tall, is not merely small at three metres. It does not exist.
Attention. The harder ceiling. Even a passer-by who could resolve the text has not agreed to read it. You are asking for a decision from someone who has other plans, so the first read has to earn the second one within about a second. Resolution you can calculate. Attention you can only design for and then test.
The tests
Each one removes something on purpose, so you can see what the poster was leaning on.

The thumbnail test. Shrink it to 60 px wide. Does anything survive besides a grey rectangle? This is also the real viewing condition for most images now.
The three-metre test. Stand back. What is readable, what is only visible, what is gone?
The one-second test. Flash it: open it, look, look away. Say out loud what it was about. If you cannot, there is no first read.
Greyscale. Strip the colour. Contrast that lived only in hue disappears.
Blur. Defocus by ten pixels. Blur is a decent stand-in for distance, and it exposes fussy edges that were doing structural work.
Cover half. Hide the image, then hide the text. If the message dies both times, neither half was carrying it — the poster only works as a complete sentence, which is a real choice, but a fragile one.


SPRINGFAIR14 JUNE, THE COMMONentry free all dayIn colourred on green — the title jumps outSPRINGFAIR14 JUNE, THE COMMONentry free all day96 vs 94255 vs 96Same poster, greyscalethe title is gone; the white line survives

The greyscale test with numbers. Left, red lettering on green: two strongly different hues, and the title reads instantly.
Right, the same poster desaturated. The green ground converts to a grey of about 96 out of 255 and the red type to about 94 — a two-step difference, invisible. The white rule and the white line below it were at 255 all along, so they survive untouched. Hue contrast without value contrast is a first read that only exists in colour, and it dies in a photocopy, a night-time street lamp, and for the roughly eight percent of men with red–green colour deficiency.




Survives the thumbnail: Flagg, 1917
Does not: Lumley, 1915


Two British and American army recruiting posters from the same war, with the same job, taking opposite bets. Both public domain.
Left (Flagg, 1917) is built for the first read. One head against an empty cream ground, the dark blue coat and hat band making a single mass, and four words in slab capitals across the bottom third at a size you can read from across a street. Cover the text and the pointing fist still says you. Cover the image and "I WANT YOU" still says it. Either half survives alone.
Right (Lumley, 1915) has almost no first read. The values are all mid-tones — brown jacket, green chair, blue carpet, tan wall — so at thumbnail size it collapses into an even mush with no shape to grab. The only text is a line of thin script at the very bottom, and it is the entire message. Cover it and the poster becomes a family photograph. This is a design that requires you to already be standing still.


The same test, other objects
Almost nothing is met at full size any more, so the poster problem has quietly spread. A book cover is a 12 mm spine on a shelf before it is a cover. A film's artwork is a 180-pixel tile in a grid of forty other tiles, and the tile is the only version most people will ever see. An app icon has to work at 40 px, which is why the good ones are one shape and one colour. A chart on a slide is read from the back of the room by people who will not ask you to zoom in.
In each case the design has a first read whether or not anyone planned it, and the test is identical: make it small, and see what is left.
What survives, roughly in order

Large areas of different value. The last thing to go, and the reason Value structure is the first thing to check.
The outline of one big shape, if it is a silhouette you already know: a head, a bottle, a mountain.
A large area of saturated colour — but as a flag, not as information.
Display type, if the capitals are tall enough. At three metres that threshold is about 4 mm — which almost every headline clears and almost no caption does.
Everything else: faces, small type, texture, fine line work, gradients.




Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Moulin Rouge: La Goulue, 1891. Public domain.
An 1891 poster that passes the squint test better than most work made this year, and the reason is that it is built from three values and nothing else. Near-black: the band of top-hatted spectators across the middle and the row of dark legs. Near-white: the dancer's petticoat, the single brightest area in the sheet and therefore the first thing you see. Mid-grey: the enormous foreground figure of Valentin, deliberately flattened to a silhouette with no interior detail at all.
Follow the yellow lamp globes as a second layer, then the red letters. Nothing here is shaded, and no edge needs resolving — which is why the design still reads at the size of a postage stamp, and why the crowd behind can be a solid black shape without anyone feeling cheated.


Common mistakes

"It's legible, I can read it." On a 27-inch monitor at 60 cm, with time. Test at the size and distance the thing will actually be met at.
"Make the logo bigger." Size is one lever among several, and the cheapest. Isolation usually beats enlargement: see Negative space.
"High contrast" meaning saturated. Saturated colours are often close in value, which is exactly the trap the greyscale diagram above shows. Contrast that matters at distance is value contrast.
Testing at 100% only. A design tuned at full size can hide a first read that never existed, because at full size everything is readable and nothing has to compete.
Treating the blur test as an insult. Blur is not a judgement on craft. It is a cheap simulation of the viewing condition, and passing it costs nothing.


Five seconds, five tests

Shrink to thumbnail. Name what you can still see.
Desaturate. Did the type stay separate from its background?
Blur heavily. Is there one dominant shape, or an even field?
Cover the text, then the image. Which half still carries the message?
Now decide whether the second read — the details, the joke, the small print — was worth putting behind that door.
